clue.text: Where to make service toll-calls?

parts.note: a toll-call sounds like a telephone charge, but here the call to a church service is made by tolling bells, which hang in church towers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Toll-calls' pretends to be about the telephone exchange; the tolling is of church bells summoning people to a service.
explanation.definitionFit: Bell towers are the places where bells are rung to call a congregation to worship.

clue.text: A cold speller — but a good novelist!

definitions.meaning: Alexander ..., a Scottish meteorologist, identified recurring cold spells in the year

explanation.walkthrough: 'Speller' means one who gives his name to spells of weather: the meteorologist Alexander Buchan's 'cold spells'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two famous Scots share the surname: a weatherman known for cold periods and the author of adventure thrillers.

clue.text: On the other hand it may be for Kathleen!

definitions.text: On the other hand it may be for Kathleen!

parts.words: On the other hand it may be for Kathleen!
parts.note: the song Kathleen Mavourneen has the line 'it may be for years, and it may be for ...', the alternative being the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: The song Kathleen Mavourneen says parting 'may be for years, and it may be for' always: the alternative 'on the other hand'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means always, completing the phrase for all time in the old ballad.

clue.text: In sight of the start.

parts.note: the phrase 'in the ___' means coming soon or visible ahead, and 'off' is the start of a race

explanation.walkthrough: Something 'in the offing' is near at hand or in view, and the word itself begins with OFF, the start of a race.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase meaning imminent or in view ahead is built on this noun for the distant sea seen from shore.

clue.text: Arid battle among fish is stupid.

annotationWithheld.why: 'Arid battle among fish is stupid.': FISH round OOL fits, but nothing in 'Arid battle' gives OOL, so the clue as held looks garbled
annotationWithheld.clue: Arid battle among fish is stupid.

clue.text: Unlucky tide-fall.

indicators.note: an unlucky fall of the tide is a mishap, so its letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: An unfortunate ebb of the tide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlucky' both signals the rearrangement of TIDEFALL and, with it, describes the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Doomed or dogged by misfortune from the start describes the hyphenated adjective.

clue.text: "Stuffs out his vacant with his form." (Shakespeare.)

definitions.text: "Stuffs out his vacant with his form." (Shakespeare.)

parts.words: "Stuffs out his vacant with his form." (Shakespeare.)
parts.note: a line from King John, where grief fills the empty clothes of a lost child, with its key word to be supplied

explanation.walkthrough: In King John, Constance says grief 'stuffs out his vacant ___ with his form', speaking of her son Arthur's empty clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means clothes, items worn on the body.

clue.text: Attention gratis, so no anxiety is

definitions.note: an adjective phrase describing a state with no worry in it

parts.note: care means attention, as in 'handle with care'
gratis means free of charge

explanation.surface: A free service with plenty of attention leaves the customer without worries.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue appears to break off after 'is'; the definition reads as 'so (that) no anxiety is (present)'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone untroubled by worry or responsibility is light-hearted, free of cares.

clue.text: Ref goes back about the wise old bird.

definitions.text: Ref goes back about the wise old bird.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the reversed ref is placed round the bird
the word ref is to be read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: ref is taken as written
the owl is proverbially the wise old bird

explanation.surface: A referee retreats around a sage old bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes back' and 'about' are the indicators. H. W. Fowler, author of Modern English Usage, is the wise old referee of correct English, so the whole clue describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: H. W. Fowler was the celebrated authority on English usage, an arbiter of language consulted like a sage.

clue.text: The solution shows a lack of balance.

definitions.text: The solution shows a lack of balance.

parts.words: The solution shows a lack of balance.
parts.note: read as accounts, a balance is money in hand, and a shortfall shows it is lacking

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lack of balance' suggests unsteadiness; in accounting it means money falling short.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortfall of income against spending leaves an account in the red.

clue.text: Lava is of help.

annotationWithheld.why: 'Lava is of help.': the answer is an anagram of LAVA IS, but no word signals the anagram and 'is' is needed both in the fodder and in the definition 'is of help'

clue.text: "They came at a" (Bunyan.)

parts.note: a quotation from Pilgrim's Progress with its missing word to be supplied: the pilgrims came to a pleasant plain called Ease

explanation.walkthrough: In Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress the pilgrims reach 'a delicate plain called Ease'; the solver fills the gap in the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: In Bunyan's older sense the word means pleasant or delightful, describing the plain called Ease.

clue.text: You can't get one for 2/6d., or can you?

definitions.text: You can't get one for 2/6d., or can you?

parts.words: You can't get one for 2/6d., or can you?
parts.note: 2/6d., two shillings and sixpence, was the old British coin called half a crown, and a small crown is also a little crown

explanation.walkthrough: Two shillings and sixpence was the half-crown, an old British coin; a small crown is a little coronet, so perhaps half a crown buys one.
explanation.definitionFit: A small crown worn by nobles is a lesser circlet below the royal crown.

clue.text: Mind not shame in such a rebuke?

indicators.note: the words mind, not and shame are to be recast in such a form as makes the rebuke

explanation.surface: Pay no heed to embarrassment when you are being told off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in such' asks for the letters of MIND NOT SHAME to be rearranged into the word for the rebuke itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprimand or warning given to someone who has done wrong is a scolding of this kind.

clue.text: The Defence Minister should, be so knowledgeable.

definitions.text: The Defence Minister should, be so knowledgeable.

parts.words: The Defence Minister should, be so knowledgeable.
parts.note: to be 'up in' a subject is to be well informed about it, and a defence minister must know about weapons

explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up in' a subject means knowing it well, so a defence minister should know all about weapons; the phrase usually means angry and protesting.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for indignant protest also reads literally as versed in weaponry.

clue.text: One would naturally expect Vera, to be.

definitions.text: One would naturally expect Vera, to be.

parts.words: One would naturally expect Vera, to be.
parts.note: the name Vera comes from the Russian for faith and resembles Latin vera, true things, so a Vera should be honest

explanation.walkthrough: Vera echoes Latin 'vera', true, so someone named Vera should live up to it by being honest.
explanation.definitionFit: Honest and never lying, a person who speaks only what is so.

clue.text: No discount and the cellarer gets note loans.

definitions.text: No discount and the cellarer gets note loans.

parts.note: selling at par means at face value, with no discount
Simon the Cellarer is the hero of a popular Victorian song
IOUs are written notes acknowledging loans

explanation.surface: A tight-fisted cellarman gives no discount and lends only against signed notes.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon the Cellarer was a Victorian comic song about a monastery's wine steward. The whole clue pictures a mean man: no discounts, and loans only on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Refusing all discounts and lending only on written promises is the behaviour of a stingy, tight-fisted person.

clue.text: Beaconsfield -.has 'the penny dropped?

indicators.note: the old penny was abbreviated d, from Latin denarius, and dropped means that letter is taken away

parts.note: Benjamin Disraeli, the Victorian Prime Minister, became Earl of Beaconsfield

explanation.surface: A question about whether the Earl has finally understood something.
explanation.walkthrough: Disraeli was born into a Jewish family; drop the D (old penny) from his name and he becomes a citizen of the Jewish state. 'Has the penny dropped' also means 'do you get it?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Disraeli's Jewish ancestry lets the clue picture him as a citizen of the modern Jewish state.

clue.text: Superior and possibly silent gadget

parts.note: U stands for upper-class or superior, in the old U and non-U distinction

indicators.note: possibly signals that silent may appear in another arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A high-quality gadget that might also run quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: In the old U and non-U distinction, U marked upper-class usage, hence 'Superior'; 'possibly' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen implement or tool is a handy device for a practical job.

clue.text: Likes a bunch of clover.

indicators.note: the letters of likes a are gathered up loosely in a bunch and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone is fond of a bunch of clover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bunch of' gathers the letters of LIKES A into a new order. Alsike is a kind of clover used for fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish clover grown for fodder bears this name, after a place in Sweden.

clue.text: How cliques gather?

parts.note: a clique is an exclusive set, so cliques gather in groups called sets

explanation.walkthrough: Split as IN SETS, the answer says how cliques gather; whole, it means pieces set into something else.
explanation.definitionFit: Small pictures or pieces placed within a larger one are additions fitted into it.

clue.text: If not the Ram, who are these official

definitions.note: the plural noun officials is what the answer means

parts.note: not is taken as written
Aries is the Ram of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Wondering who these office-holders are, if they are not star-sign Rams.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as printed ends 'official'; the setter meant 'officials', giving a plural noun to match the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawyers who authenticate deeds and witness signatures are public office-holders of this kind.

clue.text: Idyllic falcon.

definitions.meaning: belonging to Tennyson's Idylls of the King, where the wizard of Arthur's court appears
a small falcon of moorland and heath

explanation.walkthrough: 'Idyllic' here means 'from Tennyson's Idylls of the King', which features Arthur's wizard.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is shared by Arthur's enchanter in Tennyson's Idylls and by a small bird of prey.

clue.text: You'll find it in the regimen upon the table.

definitions.text: You'll find it in the regimen upon the table.

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words regimen upon, bridging them

explanation.surface: A diet plan is laid on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points inside 'regimen upon', where the four letters span the two words; a diet regimen is a bill of fare on the table.
explanation.definitionFit: A list of dishes laid on a dining table is a bill of fare.

clue.text: Trumped when 3 loses a pound.

indicators.note: loses means the pound sign letter is taken away from the cross-referenced answer

parts.note: 3 refers to the answer at 3 down
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A card was trumped when someone lost a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: '3' points to 3 down; 'loses' removes L from RUFFLED. In card games to ruff is to play a trump.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge and whist, to ruff is to play a trump card on a trick of another suit.

clue.text: 12 across? Say it with flowers!

indicators.note: say it in another way, with the letters of the cross-referenced word put in a fresh order

parts.note: 12 across refers to the answer at 12 across

explanation.surface: A florist's slogan, 'say it with flowers', attached to a cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say it with' asks for the letters of the 12 across answer, AVAILS, to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage plants grown in gardens for their bright spikes of bloom belong to this genus.

clue.text: Our tiles are detached ones.

indicators.note: the letters of our tiles come loose and are set back down in a new order

explanation.surface: Some of our roof tiles have come away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are detached' rearranges the letters of OUR TILES; tiles that come loose from a roof are themselves detached pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In geology and statistics the word names a piece or value lying apart from the main body.
